name: Saxon Math
line: Saxon teaches from a book in a fixed order, and the adult checks the work. In AMP, every answer sets the next problem.
description: AMP vs Saxon Math: Saxon teaches from a book in a fixed order and tests every fifth lesson. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous.
verdict: Saxon Math teaches one small idea a lesson from a printed book, mixes review of earlier lessons into every problem set, and tests after every fifth lesson, with the adult checking the work [1][6][8]. In AMP, assessment is continuous: every answer is checked at once, updates the learner's level and sets the next problem. Each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer.

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test. Every answer updates the learner's level in that part of math and sets the next problem: new work within reach, a gap to close, or an old skill due back. Saxon assesses with a cumulative test after every fifth lesson [7][8], and the adult grades it by hand [6].

reasons.title: Feedback on every answer
reasons.body: After every answer, AMP shows whether it was right, the correct answer and the worked steps. In Saxon, a wrong answer waits until the adult checks the work by hand, with a solutions manual [6]. Across 40 studies of computer feedback, feedback that explains had the largest average effect [15].

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything hangs off the problem: a hint that gives the first step, a lesson with a worked example, a film where there is one, the worked answer afterward, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In Saxon the unit is the lesson: one small new idea taught in text with worked examples, then practice [6][7]. Its newer books print beside each mixed problem the number of the lesson that taught it [6].

reasons.title: Continuous review
reasons.body: In AMP, learned skills come back in ordinary practice, at growing intervals, mixed with other math. Each answer sets the next problem, and an old skill due back is one of the choices. Saxon also reviews continually: every problem set mixes the new lesson with earlier ones, in the order the book prints for every student [1][8]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [13].

reasons.title: A level for each part of math
reasons.body: AMP keeps a separate level for each part of math, so a learner further along in one part than another gets work at both levels. A Saxon learner works through one book, lesson by lesson, in the book's order, and the adult sets the pace [4][6].

reasons.title: Moving on, and going back
reasons.body: In AMP a skill counts when the learner gets it right without help, more than once. Repeated misses send practice back to what the skill builds on. Saxon's test books include a Test Analysis Form that maps missed test problems to the lessons that taught them, and the adult does the reteaching [6].

rows.start: A placement test, linked from the kit's retail page [4]. The adult picks the book.
rows.teaching: A written lesson on one small new idea, with worked examples [6][7]. In kindergarten through grade 3, a parent teaches from a scripted manual [5].
rows.next: The next lesson in the book, in order. The adult sets the pace [4][6].
rows.mastery: A cumulative test after every fifth lesson, checked by the adult [6][8].
rows.review: Mixed review of earlier lessons in every problem set, fixed in the book, the same for every student [1][8].
rows.print: All print: textbook, tests and a solutions manual. The same book for every learner [4].
rows.adult: Teaches each lesson from a script in kindergarten through grade 3 [5]. From grade 4, checks daily work and tests by hand [6].
rows.reports: Paper tests, graded by hand. A Test Analysis Form maps missed test problems to the lessons that taught them [6].
rows.evidence: What Works Clearinghouse: mixed effects, grades 1 to 8 [8]. Evidence for ESSA: Promising, grades 1 and 2 [10]. Algebra I: no discernible effects [9].

theirs: Saxon Math is a print curriculum from HMH, from kindergarten through calculus [1][3]. It began with John Saxon, who taught math at Rose State College, and HMH says Saxon textbooks have been used since 1981 [2]. HMH describes its practice as distributed through the year, with continual review of earlier lessons [1].

From grade 4, a lesson opens with facts and mental math, then teaches one small new idea in text with worked examples [6][7]. Practice on that idea follows, then a mixed set of problems from earlier lessons, and a cumulative test follows every fifth lesson [7][8]. Most students read the lessons on their own, in order, and the adult checks daily work and tests with a solutions manual [6]. In kindergarten through grade 3, a parent teaches each lesson from a scripted manual, usually with manipulatives [5].
credit: Review of earlier lessons in every problem set, built into the books for decades [1][2].
A worked example with each new idea [6][7].
Outcome research in schools, including a federal randomized trial [8].

theirs: The What Works Clearinghouse's May 2017 report on Saxon's primary courses found 26 eligible studies. Five met its standards, all with reservations, covering 8,855 students in grades 1 to 8. Its rating is mixed effects, with an average gain of 8 percentile points, ranging from −1 to +16 across studies [8]. Only one was a randomized trial. In the others, groups were not assigned at random. Their effects ran from +0.11 to +0.41, and none was statistically significant as the Clearinghouse calculated it [8].

The randomized trial, by Agodini and colleagues for the Institute of Education Sciences, assigned four curricula to schools at random [8]. After two years, second graders using Saxon scored 0.25 standard deviations above those using Investigations, and about the same as those using Math Expressions (−0.02) or Scott Foresman–Addison Wesley (0.00). Pooled, the effect was +0.07 and not statistically significant. Saxon teachers gave about six hours of math a week, against about five in the other curricula [8]. Evidence for ESSA rates Saxon Math Promising for grades 1 and 2, on a 2010 paper from the same trial, with an average effect of +0.11 [10].

For Algebra I the Clearinghouse found no discernible effects (two studies, 198 students), and no study of Saxon Geometry, Algebra II or Advanced Math met its standards [9]. HMH's own summaries claim Strong evidence for kindergarten through grade 5 and Promising for grades 9 to 12 [11][12]. The first rests on the same trial's one-year result for second graders against Scott Foresman–Addison Wesley; after two years the Clearinghouse found no difference between the two [8][11]. The second rests on a 1997 study of 120 juniors that the Clearinghouse found does not meet its standards [9][12]. We found no outcome study of Saxon used at home in the Clearinghouse's or Evidence for ESSA's records.
ours: In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% on the researchers' test a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [13]. A meta-analysis of 317 experiments in verbal recall found that spacing study sessions improves retention, and that the best gap between sessions grows with how long the material must be remembered [14]. AMP applies both at every problem.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and the code is public.

them: You want to teach from a printed book, with lessons in a fixed order and review built into every problem set.
amp: You want every answer checked at once and followed by the worked steps.
You want each problem, and each review, chosen from your child's own answers.
Your child is at different levels in different parts of math.
You want to see the actual problems behind every number, without grading by hand.
You want paper too: workbooks made for your child, with worked answer keys.

questions.question: How is AMP different from Saxon Math?
questions.answer: Saxon teaches one lesson at a time from a printed book, mixes review into every problem set, and tests after every fifth lesson, with the adult checking the work [1][6][8]. AMP has no separate test: every answer is checked at once and sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does Saxon Math work?
questions.answer: In the What Works Clearinghouse's 2017 review, Saxon had mixed effects in grades 1 to 8, with an average gain of 8 percentile points [8]. Evidence for ESSA rates it Promising for grades 1 and 2 [10]. For Algebra I the Clearinghouse found no discernible effects [9].

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. They are separate programs. A learner can keep Saxon's lessons and practice in AMP, which places them from their first answers.
